domain: Religious Studies / Jewish Law / Textual Preservation
topic_summary: Analysis of the rabbinic preservation of Temple sacrifice law (Seder Kodashim) across 1,900 years without performance. The Mishnaic order details sacrificial regulations compiled after the Second Temple's destruction (70 CE), creating a contested kernel: is continuous study of unperformable ritual law an exercise of living commitment or archival preservation of a defunct system? The tension collapses the boundary between performative legal obligation and historical documentation.

key_entities: Seder Kodashim (fifth order of Mishnah/Talmud, 11 tractates on Temple sacrifice)
Second Temple (destroyed 70 CE, ending sacrificial practice)
Maimonides (12th century, codified all commandments including Kodashim in Mishneh Torah)
Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi (redacted Mishnah c.200 CE, 130 years post-Temple)
Babylonian Talmud (brief commentary on Kodashim vs other orders)
Palestinian Talmud (no commentary on Kodashim except one tractate)
Contemporary yeshivot (study Kodashim for messianic restoration preparation)
key_tensions: Study-as-substitution vs study-as-preparation (cosmic repair now vs messianic readiness later)
Maimonides' internal contradiction (Guide: sacrifices as idolatry-ruse; Mishneh Torah: literal restoration)
Neglect vs preservation (most generations ignored Kodashim; Maimonides insisted on comprehensive study)
key_mechanisms: Mishnaic codification (200 CE): oral traditions frozen in text to prevent loss
Study-as-performance doctrine: 'as if the Temple were built in their day' transforms reading into ritual enactment
key_absences: No practical halakhic application for 1,900 years (acknowledged even by practitioners)
Palestinian Talmud's near-total silence on Kodashim (only Chullin receives commentary)

axiom_contradictions.basis: Performance reading requires that study enacts cosmic repair now (Temple-independent efficacy); archive reading requires that study documents a past system with no present function. No coherent framework can hold both: either study performs the law's purpose or it does not.

Preparation reading requires Temple restoration as structurally necessary future event (study is instrumental to that telos); archive reading requires Temple restoration as structurally impossible or undesired (study is memorial only). No coherent framework can hold both: either restoration is the system's telos or it is not.
